--- title: "Universal differential equations" subtitle: "Appendix A04 · learning a transmission closure" course-unit: a04-universal-differential-equations status: complete --- ## Why this unit matters - Mechanistic SIR models fix the **functional form** of transmission; data may not agree with that choice. - A *universal differential equation* (UDE) keeps the trustworthy bookkeeping and replaces one uncertain term with a trainable **universal approximator** [@rackauckas2020]. - We differentiate **through** the ODE solver to fit the hybrid model, then ask the sharpest possible question: does the network recover the *known* closure? ::: {.notes} The message of the deck is the grey-box philosophy: impose what you trust (conservation, recovery, flow structure) and learn only what you do not (the force of infection). Emphasise that the appendix is deliberately built around a known ground truth so the fit can be validated against it, which is rarely possible with real data but ideal for teaching. ::: ## The grey-box model Keep the SIR flow, learn the force of infection $\lambda_\theta$: $$ \frac{dS}{dt} = -\lambda_\theta(I)\,S,\quad \frac{dI}{dt} = \lambda_\theta(I)\,S - \gamma I,\quad \frac{dC}{dt} = \lambda_\theta(I)\,S . $$ - **Deterministic** dynamics, **continuous** time and state, **population** level. - Data are generated from the true mass-action closure $\lambda^\star(I) = \beta c\, I = 0.5\,I$ (course baseline in proportions). - $\mathcal{N}_\theta$ supplies *only* the transmission term; $\gamma I$ and the flow structure are imposed by hand. ::: {.notes} Stress that $C$ is a cumulative-incidence tracker: daily incidence is $N\,\Delta C$, which is what we actually observe. The classification line is the same contract every chapter uses — deterministic / continuous / population. ::: ## Fit by differentiating through the solver - Loss: Poisson negative log-likelihood of daily incidence $\mu_k(\theta) = N[C(t_{k+1})-C(t_k)]_\theta$ against noisy counts $y_k$. - Gradients: reverse-mode adjoint (`InterpolatingAdjoint` + `ReverseDiffVJP`) from `SciMLSensitivity.jl`. - Optimiser: a short `Adam` run to make fast progress, then `BFGS` to polish. - Network: `Lux.Chain(Dense(1,5,tanh), Dense(5,1,softplus))` — **16 parameters**; `softplus` output guarantees $\lambda_\theta \ge 0$. ::: {#a04-slide-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using OrdinaryDiffEq, Distributions, StableRNGs, Random using Lux, DiffEqFlux, SciMLSensitivity using Optimization, OptimizationOptimisers, OptimizationOptimJL using CairoMakie N = 1000.0; βc = 0.5; γ = 0.25 u0 = [0.99, 0.01, 0.0]; tspan = (0.0, 40.0); δt = 1.0; train_time = 30.0 function sir_true!(du, u, p, t) S, I, C = u; λ, ν = p du[1] = -λ*S*I; du[2] = λ*S*I - ν*I; du[3] = λ*S*I end sol_true = solve(ODEProblem(sir_true!, u0, tspan, [βc, γ]), Tsit5(); saveat = δt) ts = 0.0:δt:train_time Ctrue = reduce(hcat, sol_true(ts).u)[3, :] data_rng = StableRNG(20240501) noisy = [rand(data_rng, Poisson(max(c, 0.0))) for c in N .* diff(Ctrue)] foi = Lux.Chain(Lux.Dense(1, 5, tanh), Lux.Dense(5, 1, softplus)) _, foi_state = Lux.setup(StableRNG(1), foi) function params_from_vector(θ) (layer_1 = (weight = reshape(θ[1:5], 5, 1), bias = θ[6:10]), layer_2 = (weight = reshape(θ[11:15], 1, 5), bias = θ[16:16])) end force_of_infection(I, θ) = foi([I], params_from_vector(θ), foi_state)[1][1] p_init = 0.1 .* randn(StableRNG(2), Float64, 16) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} This cell mirrors the book chapter kernels exactly so slides, book, and notebook stay in sync. It is executed but its output is hidden; only the two result cells below are shown to the audience. ::: ## Training the hybrid model ::: {#cell-a04-slide-train .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function sir_ude!(du, u, θ, t) S, I, C = u; λ = force_of_infection(I, θ) du[1] = -λ*S; du[2] = λ*S - γ*I; du[3] = λ*S end prob_ude = ODEProblem(sir_ude!, u0, (0.0, train_time), p_init) predict(θ) = Array(solve(prob_ude, Tsit5(); p = θ, saveat = δt, sensealg = InterpolatingAdjoint(autojacvec = ReverseDiffVJP()))) loss(θ) = (μ = max.(N .* diff(predict(θ)[3, :]), 1e-6); sum(μ .- noisy .* log.(μ))) optf = OptimizationFunction((θ, _) -> loss(θ), Optimization.AutoZygote()) res_adam = solve(OptimizationProblem(optf, p_init), OptimizationOptimisers.Adam(0.05); maxiters = 120) res = solve(OptimizationProblem(optf, res_adam.u), OptimizationOptimJL.BFGS(); maxiters = 40) θ_hat = res.u round(res.objective; digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {#a04-slide-train .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` -1730.4 ``` ::: ::: - A short, deterministic run (fixed `StableRNG` seeds) keeps the deck fast while still converging — the polished loss is reported above. ::: {.notes} The deck uses slightly fewer iterations than the book (120 Adam + 40 BFGS vs 150 + 50) purely so the slides render quickly; the closure still recovers the truth to within a few times 1e-3 over the observed range. ::: ## Validation: recovering the known closure ::: {#cell-fig-a04-slide-recovery .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} Igrid = 0.0:0.005:0.5 λ_nn = [force_of_infection(I, θ_hat) for I in Igrid] Imax = maximum(reduce(hcat, sol_true(ts).u)[2, :]) in_range = Igrid .<= Imax max_abs_error = maximum(abs.(λ_nn[in_range] .- βc .* Igrid[in_range])) fig = Figure(size = (900, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "infectious proportion I", ylabel = "force of infection λ", title = "Learned closure (max error ≈ $(round(max_abs_error; sigdigits = 2)))") lines!(ax, Igrid, βc .* Igrid; color = :black, linewidth = 2, label = "true βc·I") lines!(ax, Igrid, λ_nn; color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2, label = "neural network") vlines!(ax, [Imax]; color = :gray, linestyle = :dot) axislegend(ax; position = :lt) fig ``` ::: {#fig-a04-slide-recovery .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` The 16-parameter network recovers the true linear force of infection up to the largest infectious proportion seen in training (dotted); beyond it the closure is unconstrained. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} The single most important slide: agreement is expected only up to the dotted line because the data never visit larger infectious proportions. This is the identifiability-is-local-to-the-data lesson made visual. ::: ## Key takeaways & caveats - **Structure buys data efficiency** — 16 parameters suffice *because* recovery and flow are mechanistic; a black box would need far more data. - **Identifiability is local** — trust the closure only over the range of $I$ the training data actually visit (left of the dotted line). - **Encode priors** — `softplus` enforces $\lambda \ge 0$; monotonicity could be added similarly. - **Cost & conditioning** — every loss evaluation is an ODE solve, every gradient an adjoint solve; stiff or larger problems need care with `sensealg`. - **APIs move fast** — current `Lux` / `DiffEqFlux` / `Optimization`; legacy `FastChain` / `sciml_train` will not run on the pinned stack. See the [book chapter](../../appendices/04-universal-differential-equations.html) for derivations, and the [DiffEqFlux](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqFlux/stable/), [Lux](https://lux.csail.mit.edu/stable/), and [SciMLSensitivity](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/) manuals for the current UDE workflow. ::: {.notes} Close by pointing to the companion Pluto notebook, which pre-trains once and lets the audience explore the closure and its extrapolation region interactively without waiting for training. The two exercises (shorter training window; deeper network) are worked in the solutions appendix. :::
